title: Sometimes I Feel Like a Motherless Child
origin: African-American spiritual from the era of slavery, carried into concert repertoire by the Fisk Jubilee Singers

pd.detail: Published 1899 in Jubilee and Plantation Songs (Oliver Ditson, Boston); the spiritual itself dates from the era of slavery and has no identifiable author.
pd.sourceEdition: Traditional melody in D minor, Frank Nordberg transcription of the anonymous spiritual (musicaviva USA collection)
pd.notes: The traditional tune is encoded, not the Burleigh concert setting or any modern recorded arrangement. Slash chords in the source (Dm/A) and its passing diminished are reduced to the engine's bar-granular vocabulary. Words are carried and cleared separately -- see each section's lyrics.pd.

notes: Common time throughout, no meter reduction needed. Confidence is medium for one reason: the source notates the descending figure on 'motherless' as a quarter-note triplet, which cannot sit on a 16th grid, so it is rendered here as quarter plus two eighths (deg 5, 4, 3 into the held tonic). Pitches, phrase lengths and the long held tonic are unchanged, and that is what carries the tune; a triplet-accurate reading has to wait for a compound-meter phase. Every section starts on the downbeat, so no pickup is dropped anywhere.

pd.detail: Anonymous African-American spiritual text from the era of slavery, in oral circulation well before 1900 and set down by the Hampton Institute collectors; no identifiable author.
pd.sourceEdition: Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute, 'Religious Folk Songs of the Negro as Sung on the Plantations', new ed. from the original edition by Thomas P. Fenner, The Institute Press, Hampton, Va., 1909
pd.notes: Cross-checked against Barton, 'Old Plantation Hymns' (Lamson, Wolffe, Boston, 1899), which prints a different text family for this tune; the Hampton wording is used throughout because it is the form this melody encoding follows.

lyrics.notes: Stanzas 1-3 of the 1909 Hampton printing, in its own order. Its eye-dialect spellings are normalised to standard spelling; no words are added, dropped or reordered. Each opening line is stated three times, and every statement runs across two bars, so line 1 covers bars 0-1, line 2 bars 2-3 and line 3 bars 4-5.

lyrics.notes: The tag line that closes each of the same three stanzas, printed as the refrain in the 1909 edition, where it is sung twice. Statement 1 runs across bars 0-1 and statement 2 across bars 2-3, the second falling through the raised 7th onto the held tonic. Eye-dialect spellings are normalised to standard spelling. The two-word call the printing sets between the verse and the refrain in every stanza is not repeated here; this arrangement carries it once, in the bridge section, which is the only structural departure from the source's stanza layout. Nothing is omitted for content -- the 1909 printing gives this song three stanzas and all three are carried.

lyrics.notes: One stanza. The call at bar 0 is the phrase the 1909 printing sets to the high leap that opens this section; the tag line then falls twice, over bars 1-2 and bars 3-4, on the same figure the refrain uses. The tag takes stanza 1's wording because this section closes the arrangement. Eye-dialect spellings are normalised to standard spelling.
